newsitem.title: DUBAI: Dubai gold market sees lift from Indian politics.
newsitem.headline: Dubai gold market sees lift from Indian politics.

text.p: India's political turmoil is expected to boost Dubai's gold demand from the subcontinent and lift prices as anxious Indians turn to gold as a safe investment, traders said on Sunday.
"The political uncertainty in India should improve demand," one Dubai trader said. "Political uncertainty will mean better prices. At times of crisis people always resort to gold buying."
Dubai is the main feeder market for gold into the subcontinent. India is the world's single largest gold market.

New Delhi's 10-month-old minority government was defeated in a parliamentary confidence vote on Friday. Faced with the threat of snap polls, squabbling politicians were engaged in frantic talks to form a new coalition.
Indian equities took a knock as market players awaited political developments for direction, with some Indian investors looking to gold as a safe haven.
But one trader said the rupee's relative stability over the past few days showed that the political drama unfolding in New Delhi would have little impact on the gold market.
"There have been doubts about the government for a long time. This isn't new and I don't think it will have much of an effect on the market," he said.
Dubai's benchmark Ten Tola (TT) bar -- 3.746 ounces of 24 carat gold -- was quoted by traders at 4,795 dirhams ($1,306) on Sunday, down from 4,825 dirhams on April 6.
On the international market, spot gold was last quoted on Saturday at $346.75/$347.25 an ounce, down from $348.70/$349.20 a week earlier.
Traders said the month-long Dubai shopping festival, which opened on March 27, continued to drive gold sales upwards.
But some said the novelty of the festival, which was held for the first time last year, was wearing off and promotions for cars and luxury items were detracting from the gold market.
"There are too many other offers out there. Everyone is offering cars, clothes, watches. The shopping festival is not having the same impact on gold sales as last year," he said.
Dubai gold traders said the Eid al-Adha holiday at the end of the haj pilgrimage season on April 17 was also expected to increase gold sales and help prices firm.

"We're seeing a lot of buyers coming from Saudi Arabia and overseas as the Eid approaches," one dealer said. "We won't be able to tell how much impact the holiday will have until it gets closer to the date, but the Eid means good business."
Traditionally, Moslems give each other presents, often gold jewellery, during Eid.
